title: Book club with Mia
description: Demo conversation (synthetic, for the demo account). Alex and Mia discuss Marcus Aurelius' Meditations, pick Camus' The Stranger for next month, compare reading on a phone versus paper, then return to Meditations.

utterances.text: Okay, official book club, meeting number two. Two members, one cheese plate.
Very exclusive. So, Meditations. Did you finish it?
Most of it. I'll be honest, the middle drags. It's the same five ideas over and over.
That's what I loved, though. It's not a book, it's his private journal. Marcus Aurelius was reminding himself, not teaching us.
Okay, that changes how I read it. Like the morning one, in book two.
Yes! Where he tells himself that today he'll meet rude, ungrateful, annoying people, and he shouldn't be surprised.
Which is the most emperor thing ever. Everyone's annoying, but I'll be gracious.
Ha. But I've actually started doing it. Before work I think, someone will be difficult today, and that's fine.
Does it work?
Kind of? And the other part I underlined was about obstacles. That whatever blocks the action becomes the action.
The obstacle is the way. Very self-help.
Right, but I needed it. I'm waiting to hear about a job and everything feels blocked.
Then the waiting is the thing you practice on. Very Stoic of you.
Okay, okay. What are we reading next month?
I was thinking Camus. The Stranger. It's short and I've never read it.
Oh, I'm in. I read The Myth of Sisyphus recently, so I'm curious what the absurd looks like as a story.
Isn't it about a guy who doesn't cry at his mother's funeral?
That's how it starts. He just doesn't perform the feelings people expect, and everyone judges him for it.
Kind of the opposite of Marcus, then. Marcus is all about doing your duty.
Ooh, that could be our whole discussion. Okay, The Stranger. Paper or phone?
Paper. I read Meditations on my phone and I kept drifting into email.
Same. I'd read one page and then I'm somehow looking at flights.
And with paper I can write in the margins. My phone highlights just disappear into some app.
Okay, rule for the club. Paper only, phones in the other room.
Deal. Wait, before we finish, can we go back to Meditations for a sec? The part about death.
The one where he says you could leave life right now, so let that decide what you do and say?
That one. It sounds grim, but it made me want to be less petty at work.
That's the best summary of Marcus Aurelius I've heard. Be less petty, you'll die someday.
Put it on the cheese plate.
